A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HyResPINN research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v2 Sections 4.1–4.4 and Appendix A report original PDE-solver errors, convergence studies and measured training times.

after.justification: v3 Sections 5.1–5.7 and Appendix A report original PDE benchmark results, computational measurements and architectural ablations.

M1.justification: The hybrid architecture is retained, but v3 reverses residual-gate initialization from 1 to 0, introduces temperature-controlled gates, and extends the isotropic RBF formulation to trainable anisotropic distances (Sections 4.1–4.2). These change the reported procedure. The Wendland polynomial itself is retained despite its C4-to-C2 relabeling.

E1.justification: v3 adds Dirichlet Allen–Cahn, Korteweg–De Vries and coupled 2D Grey–Scott evaluations. Periodic Allen–Cahn and smooth/rough Darcy remain, although the smooth Darcy manufactured targets change. Chaotic Kuramoto–Sivashinsky remains, while v2's separately reported regular scenario is absent.

E2.justification: The overall baseline suite remains. However, the periodic Allen–Cahn depth comparison adds PINN and ExpertPINN to the existing comparators (v2 Figure 5; v3 Figure 8). The reported Kuramoto–Sivashinsky comparison expands from ExpertPINN alone to all five main baselines (v3 Table 7).

E3.justification: v3 adds parameter-budget comparisons and three efficiency metrics. Kuramoto–Sivashinsky now explicitly uses time-marching, with a mini-batch policy replacing v2's full-batch rule for non-Allen–Cahn problems. Timing hardware changes from A100 to H100. Smooth Darcy rows also reverse their Dirichlet/Neumann labels between v2 Table 1 and v3 Table 2; this does not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained component, depth and collocation-count studies, v3 adds systematic kernel-family and center-density ablations, joint gate-initialization sweeps, temperature/regularization studies, and gate-evolution analyses across PDEs. Appendix A and the new support-map analyses substantially expand the evidence about architectural choices and adaptation.

E5.justification: v2 reports five-trial means without numerical uncertainty in its tables. v3 retains five trials but systematically reports standard deviations for errors and throughput in Tables 3–9 and for appendix measurements in Tables 10–11. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in run count.

E6.justification: Results expand to new PDEs and ablations. Chaotic Kuramoto–Sivashinsky changes from HyResPINN 64.50% versus ExpertPINN 3.272% in v2 to 8.12e-4 versus 1.57e-3 in v3 Table 7 under revised training. Periodic Allen–Cahn's HyResPINN summary changes from 9.62e-5 to 1.19e-5. New Grey–Scott results favor StackedPINN for u and ExpertPINN for v. These are revised or additional results, not controlled same-setting gains.

T1.justification: v3 adds anisotropic distance definitions, positive-definite matrix parameterization, and mathematical definitions of parameter, computational and combined efficiency (Equations 19–20). These are limited formal additions; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs for HyResPINN.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion recast the contribution around function-space richness, progressive capacity activation and efficiency per degree of freedom. v2 primarily emphasized hybrid approximation of smooth/non-smooth features, convex residual blending and regularization. The new efficiency and initially minimal-capacity claims substantially change the central contribution framing.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the unsuccessful-Kuramoto–Sivashinsky interpretation with successful time-marched chaotic modeling, adds a stiffness/coupling explanation for weaker Grey–Scott performance, and explicitly discusses tuning costs and higher-dimensional scalability limits. Gate-evolution interpretations are extensively added, although their assignment of RBF/DNN dominance conflicts with Equation 11.

D1.justification: The reported implementation changes from LibTorch 1.11/A100 to JAX 0.6.0/H100, and a repository link replaces the promise of future code release. v3 adds RBF initialization details, parameter counts and reference-solver/data-generation instructions in Appendices A–F. However, v2 Appendix C's consolidated hyperparameter table is removed.

R1.justification: A substantial new Related Work section positions HyResPINNs against classical adaptivity, basis enrichment, kernel methods and operator learning. Added references include NeurBF, deep RBF networks and adaptive FEM literature; earlier PIRBN/kernel-network references such as Bai et al. and Fu et al. disappear. Positioning shifts toward jointly addressing richness, adaptivity and parameter efficiency.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and contribution list are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes a separate section, retained experiments are reorganized around expressivity/adaptivity/efficiency, and appendices are rebuilt by PDE. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v3 adds detailed efficiency tables, kernel/gate ablation displays, support maps and new solution/error panels, and redraws architectural illustrations. Retained figures are enlarged or relocated, including v2 Figure 4 becoming v3 Figure 7. The wall-clock panel from v2 Figure 6 and the old hyperparameter table are removed.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2, v3 provides substantially broader tests, diagnostic ablations, uncertainty reporting and reference-solver details. However, its new efficiency equations divide by Ttrain despite defining it as iterations per second, thereby rewarding lower throughput. Its gate interpretations also reverse Equation 11's RBF/DNN weighting. These inconsistencies affect the central new efficiency and adaptivity claims, so the benefits and harms do not support a reliable net quality judgment.
